subject: Medicine
summary: Fluid balance is the net difference between intake and output, governed by Starling forces. In low‑resource hospitals, clinical assessment and simple tests guide management of dehydration, overload and third‑space loss.

sections.p: Fluid balance reflects the net gain or loss of water and electrolytes. Diagnosis relies on history, physical signs, weight change and basic labs when available.
b: Intake (oral, enteral, IV, metabolic)
Output (urine, feces, insensible, drains, vomiting, diarrhoea)

t.b: Assess volume status; <0.5 mL/kg/h suggests hypovolaemia
Hyponatraemia or hypernatraemia indicates water/electrolyte imbalance
Rises with oliguria or acute kidney injury
>1.030 suggests dehydration; <1.010 suggests over‑hydration
Gain >2 kg/24 h or loss >2 kg/24 h signals fluid overload or deficit

sections.p: Fluid status is staged by clinical signs and simple measurements, guiding urgency of intervention.
b: Mild: dry mucous membranes, mild tachycardia
Moderate: hypotension, oliguria, altered mental state
Severe: shock, pulmonary oedema, anuria

t.b: >0.9 indicates circulatory compromise
>12 mmHg suggests fluid overload

sections.p: In East Africa, common causes span infections, chronic diseases and local practices.
b: Infectious: malaria, bacterial sepsis, diarrhoeal diseases
Chronic: HIV, TB, sickle cell, schistosomiasis
Cardiovascular: rheumatic heart disease, hypertension
Renal: glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome
Lifestyle: herbal remedies, alcohol
Trauma: burns, haemorrhage

t.b: Confirms malaria‑related haemolysis and hypovolaemia
Identifies bacterial sepsis causing capillary leak
Detects proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome

sections.p: Clinical features vary with the direction of fluid shift.
b: Dehydration: dry tongue, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, orthostatic hypotension
Fluid overload: peripheral oedema, ascites, pulmonary crackles, jugular venous distension

t.b: Systolic BP drop >20 mmHg on standing indicates volume depletion
Deep, laboured respiration seen in severe metabolic acidosis or fluid overload

sections.p: Use the simplest tests that answer specific questions; when unavailable, rely on bedside assessment.

t.b: Detects anaemia contributing to hypovolaemia
Rules out malaria as cause of haemolysis
Guide fluid and electrolyte replacement
Shows pulmonary oedema or effusion

sections.p: Certain signs predict imminent deterioration and require urgent action.
b: Unconsciousness, severe hypotension, oliguria, pulmonary crackles, sudden weight gain >2 kg/24 h

t.b: Immediate fluid resuscitation and source control
Avoid diuretics if hypovolaemic; use oxygen and diuretics if fluid overloaded

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct fluid imbalance with careful monitoring.
b: Rehydration: oral rehydration salts for mild–moderate; isotonic crystalloid (normal saline or Ringer’s lactate) for severe
Diuretics: furosemide only if fluid overload and adequate renal perfusion
Blood products: transfuse packed cells if Hb <7 g/dL in stable patients; avoid in hypovolaemic shock

t.b: Preferred for resuscitation; avoids hyperchloraemic acidosis
Used when pulmonary oedema is present and urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h
Avoid if patient is hypovolaemic; risk of TRALI

sections.p: Regular reassessment of intake/output, weight and signs prevents recurrence.
b: Daily weight checks
Monitor urine output
Educate on oral rehydration
Vaccinate against malaria and hepatitis B

t.b: Tracks daily intake and output; flags imbalance early

sections.p: Differential includes conditions that mimic fluid imbalance.
b: Hypothyroidism (dry skin, cold intolerance)
Cushing’s syndrome (central obesity, hypertension)
Heart failure (pulmonary oedema)

t.b: Look for purple striae, moon face; not due to fluid overload alone

sections.p: Certain tests may give false readings in this setting.
b: Serum sodium can be normal in early dehydration due to hyperglycaemia
Urine specific gravity may be low in over‑hydration but still normal if kidneys are failing

t.b: Correct for every 100 mg/dL glucose; may overestimate hyponatraemia

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration with hypotension, oliguria, altered mental state
Shock unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation

faq.q: How do I estimate fluid loss in a patient with diarrhoea when I cannot weigh them?
faq.a: Count stool volume, estimate insensible loss by body surface area, and use urine output as a surrogate.

faq.q: What is the safest crystalloid in a patient with renal impairment?
faq.a: Ringer’s lactate is preferred over normal saline to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis.

faq.q: When can I safely give diuretics in a patient with pulmonary oedema?
faq.a: Only if urine output is >0.5 mL/kg/h and the patient is haemodynamically stable.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with malaria presents with oliguria and hypotension. What is the first step? — Start isotonic crystalloid resuscitation and treat malaria with artemisinin‑based therapy.
A patient with severe dehydration shows a urine specific gravity of 1.015. What does this indicate? — The patient is likely over‑hydrated or has impaired concentrating ability; reassess fluid status.
You suspect TRALI after a blood transfusion. Which sign is most specific? — Acute hypoxaemia with bilateral infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion.

A child with sickle cell disease has sudden weight gain and crackles. What is the likely complication? — Acute chest syndrome; treat with antibiotics, oxygen and consider diuretics if fluid overloaded.
You have a patient with oliguria and rising creatinine. What is the next best investigation? — Urinalysis for proteinuria and casts to assess for acute tubular necrosis.
A patient with severe malaria has a serum sodium of 130 mmol/L. What should you correct? — Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia; adjust sodium after correcting glucose.
